Any details you care to share as advisement for those who confronted by non-compete clauses in contracts or articles with advisement you might recommend people read?

Each state has its own rules for what makes a non-compete clause enforceable. Do keep in mind that sometimes judges ignore those rules, despite supreme court rulings in your state. Whoever is paying your legal fees will need to measure whether or not appealing the verdict in such incidents is worth it. In other states they are illegal.

I live in PA and the PA supreme court ruled that there are six things, all of which must be in the contract, for it to be enforceable. Some of these I would assume hold true in other states. I don't remember exactly what all of the rules are but I will list what I can remember.

  • Consideration - What this means is monetary compensation. One month's salary is considered sufficient - this applies if you already have the job. Employment of the job is valid consideration. One other thing that is taken into account for those who are already employed is change in employment status - going part time to full time is valid consideration.
  • Trade Secrets - In restaurants these would be special sauces or rubs - like KFC's colonel's secret recipe.
  • Specialized Training - If the company has paid for specialized training or education.
  • Geographic location - The location of companies you can't go to has to be localized. You can't tell someone they can't work across the country.
  • The amount of time the agreement is in effect. - It can't be unreasonable.

I can't remember the last one, but I do remember courts look disfavorably upon agreements that restrict someones ability to earn a living. I made sure to let the judge know that I would be a burden on the system to the fullest extent of my capabilities if I didn't have a job. I drove that point home hard. I can only speak vaguely about the outcome as it was settled out of court. I did get to keep my job, with restrictions - which works on the honor system.
